title: Surge-rain dependence at 30 US tide gauges rose from 1948-1980 to 1981-2012 but did not rise further in 2013-2025, against the trend reported by Wahl et al. (2015)
abstract: Wahl et al. (2015) reported that the dependence between storm surge and heavy rain increased at many US coastal cities, with data to 2012. We repeated their method at the same 30 tide gauges (UHSLC hourly sea level, extended with NOAA CO-OPS to 2025; GHCN-Daily rain within 25 km) and used 2013-2025 as an out-of-sample test. Surge is the residual of yearly harmonic tide fits. Case I pairs the annual largest surge with rain within one day; Case II pairs the annual largest rain with surge within one day. We compare the mean site Kendall tau in 1948-1980, 1981-2012 and 2013-2025 with a joint year bootstrap, for three rain series and two event samples. The spatial pattern reproduced: Case I dependence was significant at 16 of 19 Gulf and East gauges. The rise before 2013 reproduced in direction in all 12 variants (+0.03 to +0.12 in tau; interval excluded zero in 6). In the primary analysis, Case II tau went from 0.074 to 0.175 and Case I from 0.168 to 0.212. After 2012 the rise did not continue: 2013-2025 tau was 0.186 (Case I) and 0.125 (Case II), and the change from 1981-2012 was -0.05 to +0.09 in all variants with intervals that include zero. Linear trend continuation predicted 0.243 and 0.245; it was the worst site-level forecast, and observed values were below it in 10 of 12 variants. Wahl's last 50-year running window rose only +0.02 and +0.01 when we added 13 years, less than the +0.03 to +0.10 their slopes imply. A denser rain network after 2007 (CoCoRaHS) raised measured Case II dependence, so all-gauge averages can make an artificial rise. Limitations: the test window has only 13 years, so a small continued rise is not excluded; our tide fits and rain stations differ from the original study.
